title: Celebrating others
hookLine: Moggallana reads the joy on Sariputta's face before a word is said: mudita, joy at another's joy
tomorrow: why did people call a holy man a glutton?

cards: A friend's name lights up the phone: I GOT IT. There's a half-second before typing congrats when anything can happen.
Two young friends in the Buddha's time, Sariputta and Moggallana, made a pact: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other.

One morning Sariputta meets a monk named Assaji, walking for alms, so calm that Sariputta has to ask who his teacher is. Assaji gives him a few lines of the Buddha's teaching, and Sariputta understands.
He walks back to his friend. And before he says a word, Moggallana sees his face.

teach.b: In the Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, Moggallana says, in effect: your face is calm, friend, your skin is bright. Have you found the deathless?

teach.h: HE SAW IT BEFORE A WORD.
teach.b: He reads the joy on his friend's face and asks about it before Sariputta says a word. No race. No "why him first".
Then Sariputta shares the verse, Moggallana understands too, and the two go to the Buddha together.
Buddhism has a word for that turn toward a friend's good: mudita, joy at another's joy.
It's one of the four boundless states the Buddha taught, beside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, and it's practiced on purpose: wishing that another's good fortune will last.
It can even be heard: in Theravada Buddhist communities, when someone does a good deed, people around them may say sadhu, sadhu, sadhu: well done, said three times. That's mudita out loud.
The teaching under it: someone else's win doesn't subtract from yours.
It adds a second joy, if you let it in. Envy shrinks the world to one winner. Mudita makes room for two, and it can be practiced, like any other skill.

how: Buddhists cultivate mudita, sympathetic joy, as one of the four brahmaviharas, often in meditation that wishes others' good fortune to last; in Theravada communities people may say 'sadhu' three times to rejoice in a good deed.

o: being truly happy about someone else's good news
throwing a big party to mark a friend's birthday
praising people so they'll think well of you

games.q: the two friends: tap the pairs.
p: the calm monk with a few lines
found it first and came back
read the joy on his friend's face

s: Moggallana asked about the news before Sariputta spoke
he saw the calm in his friend's face first.
mudita means pity for someone's suffering
that's compassion. mudita is joy at someone's joy.
in Buddhist teaching, mudita is a feeling you either have or don't
it's one of the four boundless states, practiced on purpose.

games.q: your younger brother gets into the program you were turned down for. he texts you first. what would mudita look like?
o: be glad with him first; your own sting can wait its turn.
congratulate him, then remind him how close you came.
wait a day to reply, so your joy for him is fully pure.
games.why: Moggallana turned toward his friend's joy before a word was said. mudita is practiced: you turn toward their good news first.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has good news right now, big or small. Write them a message that's only about their joy: no "me too", no advice, no comparison. Read it once, slowly, and let their good news be good.

wordCard.voice: Celebrating others: mudita, joy at someone else's joy, one of the four boundless states in Buddhist teaching.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: sympathetic joy, joy at another's joy.

carryVoice: Your line: glad for you. Moggallana saw his friend's joy before a word was said. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga I.23-24 (Sariputta meets Assaji; Moggallana sees his face; both go to the Buddha)
Digha Nikaya 13, Tevijja Sutta (the four boundless states: love, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity)
Theravada custom: 'sadhu, sadhu, sadhu' in rejoicing at a good deed
